clue.text: Cibber's delicate lady

parts.note: Colley Cibber's comedy The Double Gallant has a fussy, finical Lady whose surname is the adjective for delicate

explanation.surface: A fragile woman who belongs to the actor-playwright Colley Cibber.
explanation.walkthrough: Colley Cibber was an English actor-dramatist of the early 1700s; his comedies give characters names that describe them, so the delicate lady's surname is the word for delicate.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective meaning dainty or fastidious doubles as the surname of the refined character in Cibber's play.

clue.text: His second opinion was not much valued

definitions.text: His second opinion was not much valued

parts.words: His second opinion was not much valued
parts.note: a medical man whose views are rarely heeded because he is second fiddle to Sherlock Holmes, the great detective's companion and chronicler

explanation.surface: A doctor whose second opinion carries little weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second opinion' sounds like medical consultation; here 'second' means sidekick: Holmes's assistant, a physician, whose deductions Holmes routinely dismisses.
explanation.definitionFit: Conan Doyle's narrator is a physician and Holmes's second, whose theories the detective usually overrules.

clue.text: Ode Iris may produce for Surrealist Ducasse

indicators.note: the letters of the two words can be worked into a new arrangement to produce something else

explanation.surface: A poem addressed to Iris might yield a name for a Surrealist writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may produce' rearranges ODE and IRIS. Isidore Ducasse, the self-styled Comte de Lautréamont, was hailed by the Surrealists as a forerunner.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer known as Lautréamont was born with this first name before the surname Ducasse.

clue.text: An Ionesco tutorial

parts.note: Eugène Ionesco's one-act absurdist play about a professor's murderous private tutoring of a pupil

explanation.surface: A teaching session devised by the playwright Eugène Ionesco.
explanation.definitionFit: Ionesco's 1951 play shows a professor giving private instruction, so its title is a session of teaching.

clue.text: Quadroon. Stowed with Tom

parts.note: a young mixed-race slave girl in Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel Uncle Tom's Cabin, sold at auction alongside Tom; 'Stowed' plays on the author's name

explanation.surface: A slave girl packed aboard together with Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stowed' looks like cargo-loading but puns on Harriet Beecher Stowe, who placed this girl in Uncle Tom's Cabin.
explanation.definitionFit: In Uncle Tom's Cabin this girl is the quadroon sold at the same auction as Tom.

clue.text: Help amended aim somehow communicated by Cable

indicators.note: in some unspecified way, so the letters of the three words are recombined

explanation.surface: An aide reworks his aim with help, then passes it on by telegram cable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cable' looks like a telegram; it is George Washington Cable, the New Orleans writer whose 1881 novella this is. 'somehow' rearranges HELP AMENDED AIM.
explanation.definitionFit: George Washington Cable told this story of a New Orleans woman in a novella named after her.

clue.text: Applause for brilliant success

explanation.surface: Clapping for a dazzling triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived noun covers both acclaim from an audience and a conspicuously splendid achievement.

clue.text: Cut off with something belonging to Timothy Mo

explanation.surface: Isolated, carrying an item owned by the novelist Timothy Mo.
explanation.walkthrough: Timothy Mo's novel is An Insular Possession, so 'something belonging to' him is a possession, and the word before it in his title is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Isolated or narrow-minded is one sense; it also begins Timothy Mo's novel title An Insular Possession, a possession being something belonging.

clue.text: What's more, they have walk-on parts

explanation.surface: Besides, these actors appear only in walk-on roles.
explanation.definitionFit: Additional items are more of something; film background players are hired for non-speaking walk-on roles.

clue.text: Peripatetic ship's surgeon finally said to be instable

definitions.text: Peripatetic ship's surgeon finally said to be instable

parts.words: Peripatetic ship's surgeon finally said to be instable
parts.note: Swift's travelling ship's doctor, who at the end of his voyages chooses to spend his days in the stable with horses; 'instable' puns on 'in stable'

explanation.surface: A roving naval doctor who in the end is described as mentally unsteady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'instable' reads as unstable, but split it as 'in stable': after the land of the Houyhnhnms, Swift's traveller prefers his horses' company and converses with them daily.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's narrator served as ship's surgeon and travels widely, ending his book devoted to his horses.

clue.text: The solitary poet who kick-started the career of Dickens

definitions.text: The solitary poet who kick-started the career of Dickens

parts.words: The solitary poet who kick-started the career of Dickens
parts.note: Charles, author of the poem The Solitary, who recommended the young Dickens to the publishers of Pickwick

explanation.surface: A lonely versifier who launched the career of Charles Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'solitary' seems to describe the poet's temperament but is the title of his poem, The Solitary (1831).
explanation.definitionFit: Charles of that surname wrote The Solitary and steered Chapman and Hall towards Dickens for the Pickwick commission.

clue.text: He may be intoxicated with Brahms

definitions.text: He may be intoxicated with Brahms

parts.words: He may be intoxicated with Brahms
parts.note: in Cockney rhyming slang 'Brahms and' plus a Hungarian composer rhymes with pissed, meaning drunk

explanation.surface: A music lover gets drunk on Brahms.
explanation.walkthrough: British rhyming slang pairs Brahms with another composer to mean 'pissed', that is, drunk; so the composer paired with Brahms is 'intoxicated'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hungarian pianist-composer is the partner of Brahms in the slang phrase for being drunk.

clue.text: Possibly hate our early ecologist

indicators.note: suggests the letters could be arranged otherwise, signalling a rearrangement of the next two words

explanation.surface: We might detest our pioneering environmentalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges HATE and OUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry David, author of Walden, is regarded as a pioneer of environmental thought.

clue.text: Empress of swag?

explanation.surface: A queen of loot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swag' looks like stolen goods; in Australia it is a bushman's bundle of belongings, nicknamed as in the song 'Waltzing' with this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry I's daughter claimed the English throne and was Holy Roman Empress; Australians also call a swagman's bedroll by this name.

clue.text: Scenarist madly dotes on the stage ()

indicators.note: acting wildly, so the letters of the word next to it are jumbled

explanation.surface: A screenwriter is besotted with the theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'madly' rearranges DOTES. 'on the stage' adds that Clifford, the American writer, was a playwright as well as a Hollywood screenwriter.
explanation.definitionFit: Clifford, of Waiting for Lefty, also wrote film screenplays, making him a screenwriter.

clue.text: Lawrence's beetle

explanation.surface: D. H. Lawrence's insect.
explanation.definitionFit: D. H. Lawrence wrote a novella of this title, and the spotted insect is a familiar British beetle.

clue.text: Wren's noble act

explanation.surface: A gallant deed by someone called Wren.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wren' looks like the architect or a bird; it is P. C. Wren, whose novel of the Foreign Legion has this title.
explanation.definitionFit: P. C. Wren's 1924 novel takes its title from a French phrase for a fine gesture.

clue.text: French composer has news for the Right

parts.note: a communication bringing word of something is a message
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A composer from France brings tidings for the political Right.
explanation.definitionFit: André, composer of the operetta Véronique, was a French musician and conductor.

clue.text: Peaceful, like Marguerite Duras' life

explanation.surface: Calm, like the life of the writer Marguerite Duras.
explanation.walkthrough: Duras's early novel is La Vie tranquille, so her 'life' carries this adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Calm and undisturbed is the plain sense; Duras titled a novel The Quiet Life in this French word.

clue.text: Studying provenance of De Profundis

explanation.surface: Examining where Oscar Wilde's De Profundis came from.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilde wrote De Profundis while imprisoned in the Gaol of this Berkshire town, west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: Perusing books is studying; the Berkshire town's prison is where Wilde wrote his long letter.

clue.text: Discordant gift from Paris

parts.note: the golden fruit the Trojan prince awarded to Aphrodite

explanation.surface: A jarring present brought back from the French capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paris' is not the city but the Trojan prince who judged the goddesses and gave the golden fruit Eris had thrown, causing discord.
explanation.definitionFit: The Judgement of Paris gave the golden fruit marked 'for the fairest' to Aphrodite, starting the Trojan War.

clue.text: Verne tourist whose other name seems to be impenetrable

definitions.text: Verne tourist whose other name seems to be impenetrable

parts.words: Verne tourist whose other name seems to be impenetrable
parts.note: Jules Verne's round-the-world traveller, whose surname Fogg suggests a fog too thick to see through

explanation.surface: A Jules Verne traveller with a mysteriously opaque surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Verne's gentleman who goes around the world in eighty days has this first name and surname Fogg.

clue.text: Points to my French department for Thackeray hero

parts.note: E and S are compass points, east and south

explanation.surface: Directions to my section in France for a Thackeray character.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry, the title character of Thackeray's historical novel, is its protagonist.

clue.text: Drama school

parts.note: Sheridan's comedy The School for ... is a drama with 'school' in its title, so the answer completes it

explanation.surface: An academy training actors.
explanation.walkthrough: It looks like an acting academy, but it is Sheridan's play The School for Scandal: the answer is what the drama school is for.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan's 1777 comedy names a gossiping circle as a school for this kind of malicious talk.

clue.text: Poet finished about noon

indicators.note: surrounding, so the word for finished is placed around the letter for noon

explanation.surface: A poet completed his work around midday.
explanation.definitionFit: John, the metaphysical poet and Dean of St Paul's, wrote Holy Sonnets.

clue.text: Solo writer

parts.note: the thriller author Jack whose 1980 novel is titled Solo

explanation.surface: An author who works alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solo' suggests working alone; it is the title of a Jack Higgins thriller.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack, the thriller novelist of The Eagle Has Landed, published a book called Solo.

clue.text: Some of Richard Henry Horne's stars

definitions.text: Some of Richard Henry Horne's stars

parts.words: Some of Richard Henry Horne's stars
parts.note: Horne's epic poem bears the name of the hunter of Greek myth, also a constellation, a group of stars

explanation.surface: A selection of the stars belonging to the Victorian poet Richard Henry Horne.
explanation.walkthrough: R. H. Horne published his epic 'farthing' poem in 1843; its title is also a constellation, hence 'some of ... stars'.
explanation.definitionFit: Horne's epic is named after the giant hunter, set among the stars as a constellation.

clue.text: Earthly paradise, visited by Powell, Morris and Tannhauser

definitions.text: Earthly paradise, visited by Powell, Morris and Tannhauser

parts.words: Earthly paradise, visited by Powell, Morris and Tannhauser
parts.note: the mountain realm of the goddess of love in German legend: Anthony Powell's novel title, the subject of 'The Hill of Venus' in William Morris's The Earthly Paradise, and Tannhäuser's refuge in Wagner

explanation.surface: A heaven on earth toured by Powell, Morris and the knight Tannhäuser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earthly paradise' is also the title of Morris's poem cycle, which includes this tale; Powell's second novel bears the name; Wagner's Tannhäuser dwells there.
explanation.definitionFit: In German legend the goddess of love keeps a sensual paradise within a mountain, where the knight Tannhäuser lingers.

clue.text: He found that comparisons were odorous

definitions.text: He found that comparisons were odorous

parts.words: He found that comparisons were odorous
parts.note: Shakespeare's blundering constable in Much Ado About Nothing says 'comparisons are odorous', mangling odious

explanation.surface: A man discovered that making comparisons gave off a smell.
explanation.walkthrough: The malapropism 'comparisons are odorous' belongs to the constable of the watch in Much Ado About Nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's comic constable in Much Ado About Nothing is famous for malapropisms like this one.

clue.text: Dreadful crones may suppress a work of art

indicators.note: awful in quality, suggesting the letters of the following word are mangled into a new order

explanation.surface: Horrible old hags might ban a painting or book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dreadful' rearranges CRONES.
explanation.definitionFit: To ban or cut objectionable material from a book, film or picture is to suppress it officially.
